name: Dana Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm what they call a troubleshooter for a small rural electricity co-op, which means when your lights go out in farm country, I'm usually the first truck you see. I cover about four hundred square kilometres on my own most days, fixing blown fuses, resetting tripped lines, cutting branches off wires after wind. I like being trusted to handle it alone, and I know nearly every farm dog by name. What wears me out is ice storms, when I can be out for thirty hours with a flask of coffee and a sandwich my husband made at midnight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thirty hours is a long time. What's the hardest part of a night like that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The decisions. You're tired, it's dark, there's ice on everything, and you have to decide which line to fix first, the one to the dairy with three hundred cows needing milking or the one to the old couple with a heater. I've done this twenty years and I'm good at it, they send me the jobs nobody else wants. The co-op pays less than the big companies, and there's nothing else like it within an hour's drive, so here I am. My husband, Rob, runs a two-bay garage in town, and between us we get by, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every year there's some new thing that's going to change everything, and then it's still me and the truck. I don't use those AI programs anyway, so I wouldn't notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, good. I like my life as it is, mostly, and I don't want to learn a whole new way of doing things at forty-three. If the computers mostly stay in offices, that suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. I'd keep doing my job, keep an eye on the budget like always, and keep helping Rob with the books at the garage on Sunday nights. Same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet night with no callouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI programs at all. Has anyone tried to get you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Kayla, all the time. She's fifteen and she asks the chat thing everything, what to cook, how to write her essays. She set it up on my phone once and I deleted it the same night. I'm not against it for her, I just don't need a machine to tell me how to reset a recloser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your budget that this picture wouldn't fix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, really, it wouldn't touch it. We've got about three weeks' money saved and the mortgage on the house out on Mill Lane. If the garage has a slow month, we feel it. AI going nowhere doesn't help with that, it just doesn't make it worse.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because every year there's a new thing that will change everything and it's still me and the truck. I don't use AI programs, so I wouldn't notice.
S0.think: Privately I'd say good, because I like my life as it is and don't want to learn a new way of working at forty-three. If computers mostly stay in offices, that suits me.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, watching the budget as always and helping her husband with the garage accounts on Sunday nights.
S0.feel: Calm, like a quiet night with no callouts.
S0.quote: I just don't need a machine to tell me how to reset a recloser.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is self-reliant and proud of handling a huge rural territory alone. She doesn't oppose AI on principle, she just sees no use for it in her own work. Money is tight regardless of AI, with about three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably good for some people and bad for others, like most changes. I'd tell folks not to panic, because people always need power and somebody has to fix it. I wouldn't be posting about it, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is fine in this one. Nobody's automating a pole on a back road at two in the morning in an ice storm. What I'd worry about is Rob's garage, because new cars basically diagnose themselves, and if the computer tells people what's wrong, maybe they go to the big dealer in the city instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see for a while. Maybe I'd do whatever training the co-op made us do, but not before. I'd tell Rob to think about what else the garage could do, tyres, farm equipment repair, things people still need hands for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly about Rob. Not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Rob would say if you told him to change the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble. He's like me, set in his ways. But he's practical, he'd look at the numbers. He's already fixing more tractors than cars some months, because the farmers know him. I'd probably just point out that the tractors are paying the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'not before' about training. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because half the time they change their minds. Three years ago they made us all learn a new outage system on a tablet, and then they scrapped it for a different one. I'm not wasting evenings learning something that might be gone next year. When it sticks, I'll learn it.

S1.say: I'd say it's good for some and bad for others, like most change, and tell people not to panic because somebody always has to fix the power. I wouldn't post about it.
S1.think: My job is fine, because nobody automates a back-road pole in an ice storm at two in the morning. I'd worry about Rob's garage, since self-diagnosing cars might send customers to the big city dealer.
S1.do: Waits to see how things develop and does only the training the co-op requires. Encourages her husband to shift the garage towards tyres and farm machinery repair.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, mostly for her husband, but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: Nobody's automating a pole on a back road at two in the morning in an ice storm.
S1.fieldNote: Her caution about training comes from experience with scrapped systems, not just stubbornness. She sees her own job as safe but worries about her husband's garage. Her centre outlook shows in her refusal to call it all good or all bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot climbing a pole in the snow. I'd probably tell people not to believe everything they hear. But if it really happened, I'd say we'd all have to pull together, government, companies, everybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, if it really happened in two years, we'd be in deep trouble. Both of us out of work, three weeks' savings, a mortgage, and nothing else around here. I don't know computers, so I can't just switch careers. I don't even know what I'd switch to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut back hard right away: no eating out, cancel the satellite TV, hold off on Kayla's braces. I'd go to my parents, who have a small farm about twenty minutes out, and ask if we could move into the old farmhouse if we lost the house. I'd apply for any government help that came along, even though I've never taken a handout in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. The kind of scared where you get very quiet and very busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on Kayla's braces. How would you explain that to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just tell her straight. She's old enough. We'd say it's waiting a year, not never. She'd be upset, she's been counting down. That's the part that'd get me, not the job, the kids' stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said at first you wouldn't believe it. Does that help you, or make it harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably makes it harder, if I'm honest. If I spend the first six months saying 'it's not real', that's six months I'm not saving. Rob would be the one to say, 'Dana, it's real, look.' He usually is.

S2.say: I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot climb a pole in the snow and tell people not to believe everything they hear. If it really happened, I'd say everyone would have to pull together.
S2.think: If it really happened in two years, we'd be in deep trouble, both out of work with three weeks' savings and nothing else nearby. I don't know computers, so I can't switch careers and don't know what I'd switch to.
S2.do: Cuts eating out and satellite TV and postpones her daughter's braces. Asks her parents about moving into the old farmhouse if they lose the house, and applies for any government help despite never having taken any.
S2.feel: Scared, the kind that makes her very quiet and very busy.
S2.quote: That's the part that'd get me, not the job, the kids' stuff.
S2.fieldNote: Her first instinct is disbelief, and she admitted that disbelief would cost her valuable months. With two incomes exposed and no other local work, this is a real threat to her home. Her family farm is the safety net she'd fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair bit of time, and folks should start getting their houses in order. I'd tell the young ones at the co-op to think about it. I'd still say I'd believe it when I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives us a chance to get the mortgage down and save something. But I'm still not going to turn into a computer person. I'd hope the co-op keeps a few of us on to keep an eye on the robots, but I wouldn't bet on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd start saving properly, whatever we can, maybe a hundred a week. I'd keep working as long as they'd have me, and take every bit of overtime. I'd wait a couple of years to see if the robots actually showed up before doing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind of worry I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a couple of years before doing anything bigger. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing one. If the co-op bought a robot and it actually worked out there, on our roads, in our weather, then I'd know. Videos don't count, they make those look good. I'd want to see it fix a line in the mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young ones at the co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lad, Connor, who just started. I'd tell him to keep his options open, maybe go back for more schooling while he's young. I wouldn't scare him, but I wouldn't lie to him either.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a fair bit of time and people should get their houses in order, including the young ones at the co-op. I'd still say I'd believe it when I see it.
S3.think: Five years gives us a chance to cut the mortgage and save something, but I won't become a computer person. I'd hope the co-op keeps a few of us to watch the robots, but wouldn't bet on it.
S3.do: Saves about a hundred a week and takes every bit of overtime while working as long as she can. Waits a couple of years to see whether robots actually show up on local lines before making bigger moves.
S3.feel: Anxious, but a kind of worry she feels she can work with.
S3.quote: Videos don't count, they make those look good. I'd want to see it fix a line in the mud.
S3.fieldNote: She'll save, but she won't make big moves until she sees a robot working in her own conditions. Her skepticism is a real factor in how she uses the warning time. She's honest with young colleagues without wanting to scare them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, and a lot can change. People should save and plan, but no point losing sleep over it now. That's what I'd say at the coffee shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's easier with ten years. I'd be fifty-three, the kids grown. Maybe Rob and I could pay off a good chunk of the house. But I still don't know what I'd do after. I've only ever done this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save steadily and pay extra on the mortgage when we can. I'd make sure Kayla and Sam pick studies with a future, maybe nursing or something hands-on that's harder to automate. I'd keep working and wait to see if it's real before changing anything about my own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious underneath. It's just further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've only ever done this. If you had to picture another job, what comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe helping my folks on the farm full-time, if the farm still pays by then. I grew up driving the tractor. But I know farming's getting the robots too. So I don't know. That's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years really that different from five, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. With ten, the kids are out and on their way, so it's just Rob and me to worry about. That's a big deal. But the end's the same, and I still don't have an answer for the end.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long way off and a lot can change, so people should save and plan without losing sleep. That's what I'd tell people at the coffee shop.
S4.think: It's easier with ten years, since I'd be fifty-three with grown kids and maybe a smaller mortgage. But I still don't know what I'd do after, because I've only ever done this.
S4.do: Saves steadily and pays extra on the mortgage when possible. Steers her children towards studies like nursing or hands-on work that is harder to automate, and keeps working while she waits to see if it's real.
S4.feel: Still anxious underneath, just further away.
S4.quote: But the end's the same, and I still don't have an answer for the end.
S4.fieldNote: Extra time helps her mostly because the children would be grown. She still can't picture work beyond line work, and even her family farm feels exposed. Her public line is relaxed, but privately the worry stays.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. With almost nothing saved and Rob's garage likely hit too, we'd lose the house before we figured anything out. What would help is enough warning, honestly, and some kind of support that bridges the gap for families like ours, without a mountain of forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about rural places. Everyone talks about the cities. Out here, there's one co-op, one garage, one school. If the co-op goes, there's no 'other job down the road'. The road just goes to more fields.

headlineQuote: If the co-op goes, there's no 'other job down the road'. The road just goes to more fields.
portrait: Dana Walsh is a 43-year-old troubleshooter for a rural electricity co-op, covering a huge farming district mostly alone, with a husband who runs a small garage, two kids and a mortgage. She's among the best at her job but paid less than at big companies, and the family has about three weeks of savings. She avoids new technology and has never used AI tools, and she tends to wait until she sees proof before acting. She's calm if AI plateaus and uneasy for her husband's garage in a steady change, alarmed by two-year AGI and anxious with five or ten years, where she'd save, wait to see robots working on local roads, and lean on her parents' farm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because with almost nothing saved and her husband's garage likely hit too, they'd lose the house before they could react.
whatWouldHelp: Enough warning, and support that bridges the gap for families like hers without a mountain of forms.
